content.text: Some real-world phenomena are impossible, impractical, or dangerous to study directly. A scientist cannot shrink to the size of a molecule to study chemical reactions. An engineer cannot crash thousands of real cars to test safety designs. A climatologist cannot wait centuries to observe global warming. Simulations solve this problem — they use computing to model complex phenomena in a controlled digital environment.

content.definition: An abstraction of a more complex object or phenomenon for a specific purpose. Uses varying sets of values to reflect the changing state of a phenomenon. Often mimics real-world events to draw inferences without the constraints of the real world.

content.text: There are two essential properties of a simulation that the CED identifies separately. First, a simulation is an ABSTRACTION — it simplifies and approximates the real thing rather than perfectly replicating it. Second, a simulation uses VARYING SETS OF VALUES to reflect how the phenomenon changes over time — the values update as the simulation progresses to model the changing state.

content.definition: When real-world events are impractical for experiments — too big, too small, too fast, too slow, too expensive, or too dangerous. Simulations facilitate the formulation and refinement of hypotheses.

content.text: Simulations often mimic real-world events with the purpose of drawing inferences, allowing investigation of a phenomenon without the constraints of the real world. The key word is 'inferences' — a simulation does not give you perfect knowledge of what will happen in the real world, but it allows you to draw conclusions and make predictions based on the model.

content.text: Simulations facilitate the formulation and refinement of hypotheses related to the objects or phenomena under consideration. This means simulations are not just used to confirm what we already know — they actively help scientists and engineers come up with new ideas and refine existing ones. A researcher runs a simulation, sees an unexpected result, forms a hypothesis about why, adjusts the simulation, and runs it again. This iterative process accelerates scientific discovery.

content.text: Simulations Are Abstractions: What Gets Left Out

content.definition: Developing a simulation involves removing specific details or simplifying functionality. Simulations can contain bias derived from the choices of real-world elements that were included or excluded.

content.text: The process of developing an abstract simulation involves removing specific details or simplifying functionality. No simulation perfectly replicates reality — it cannot. Every simulation involves choices about what to include and what to leave out. These choices determine both the usefulness and the limitations of the simulation.

rows: Climate simulation using Northern Hemisphere data only
Northern Hemisphere atmospheric patterns, temperature, precipitation
Excludes Southern Hemisphere weather patterns and ocean currents
Predictions may be biased toward Northern Hemisphere conditions — may inaccurately predict global trends
Traffic simulation using average driver speed
Vehicle positions, speed limits, intersection timing
Excludes individual variation in driver behavior, road rage, distracted driving
May not capture realistic traffic jams caused by a single slow or erratic driver
Disease spread simulation ignoring social networks
Population density, infection probability, recovery rate
Excludes family clusters, workplace transmission, superspreader events
May underestimate how fast the disease spreads through highly connected social groups
Hurricane simulation ignoring deep ocean temperatures
Surface water temperature, wind patterns, atmospheric pressure
Excludes sub-surface ocean heat content
May inaccurately predict storm intensity — deep warm water is a key fuel source for hurricanes

content.text: Simulations can contain bias derived from the choices of real-world elements that were included or excluded. This is directly connected to the data bias concept from Unit 2. The choices about what to model and what to leave out are made by the developers, and those choices can reflect biases — intentional or not. A simulation that only models certain populations, certain conditions, or certain factors will produce results that are biased toward those choices.

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Students sometimes think that because a simulation uses real data or real physics, it cannot be biased. This is wrong. Bias in simulations comes from the CHOICES about what to include and exclude — not from mathematical errors. A simulation built only with data from wealthy urban hospitals is biased, even if the math is perfect.

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: A simulation being imperfect does NOT make it useless. ALL simulations simplify reality — that is the nature of abstraction. A simulation that excludes some details can still provide extremely valuable insights and help scientists formulate and test hypotheses. The key is understanding what was included and excluded so you can interpret results appropriately.

content.term: How do simulations use random values?
content.definition: Random number generators can be used in simulations to simulate the variability that exists in the real world, making the simulation more realistic.

content.text: Real-world phenomena are not perfectly predictable. Weather varies unpredictably. People make different choices at different times. Equipment fails at random moments. Diseases spread with a probability — not a certainty — per contact. Random number generators allow simulations to model this natural variability, making the simulation more realistic than a purely deterministic model would be.

content.code:
-- Disease spread simulation using random values:
-- Each contact between an infected and healthy person has a 30% chance of transmission

INFECTION_PROBABILITY ← 3   -- 30% chance = RANDOM(1,10) ≤ 3

PROCEDURE simulateContact(isInfected)
{
   IF(isInfected)
   {
      roll ← RANDOM(1, 10)
      IF(roll ≤ INFECTION_PROBABILITY)
      {
         RETURN true    -- transmission occurred
      }
   }
   RETURN false         -- no transmission
}

-- Without random values:
-- Every contact would ALWAYS transmit or NEVER transmit
-- The simulation would not reflect real-world probabilistic spread

-- With random values:
-- Each contact has a 30% chance of transmission
-- Reflects the probabilistic nature of real disease transmission
-- Different runs produce different outcomes — like real epidemics

Not all drivers behave identically — variation causes real traffic patterns
